opus-5.5.text:
I think the gap is quite large, and people often underestimate it.

With language data, cleaning is relatively cheap per token. A lot of the work can be done with heuristics, deduplication, small classifiers, perplexity filters, maybe a lightweight model to score quality. Text is compact. A web page might be a few thousand tokens, and you can process billions of documents with a reasonable CPU cluster plus some GPU time for the model-based filters.

Multimodal is a different story. First, the raw data is just much heavier. An image is far more bytes than a paragraph, and video is orders of magnitude more than images. Simply decoding, storing, and moving the data around becomes a real cost before you even start judging quality.

Second, the filtering itself almost always needs neural models. With text you can sometimes get away with rules. With images or video, to know whether the caption matches the content, whether a frame is blurry, whether there's a watermark, whether it's unsafe, whether a clip has meaningful motion, you need to run vision encoders, sometimes even a full vision-language model to recaption. Recaptioning in particular is expensive, because you're doing generation, not just classification. In some pipelines the compute spent on preparing data starts to approach a meaningful fraction of the training compute itself.

Third, alignment is the hard part. In language, the data is its own label. In multimodal, the value lies in how well the text and the image or video correspond. Raw alt-text from the web is noisy, short, often irrelevant. So you're not just filtering, you're often rewriting the supervision signal, and that's where a lot of the cost goes.

So my rough feeling is that per unit of useful training signal, multimodal cleaning can be one or even two orders of magnitude more expensive than text, and for video it's even worse. That's also why I think data engineering in multimodal is still an underappreciated source of competitive advantage. The teams that build efficient pipelines, using cheap filters first and only sending the promising candidates to the expensive models, a kind of cascade, can afford to look at far more data and end up with much better quality.

r001.rationale: The response says multimodal cleaning is much more expensive than language cleaning and that video is even worse.

r002.rationale: The response says multimodal cleaning can cost one or two orders of magnitude more than text; it does not describe non-video multimodal cleaning as roughly comparable in cost.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think people underestimate this by a lot. When we talk about cleaning language data, the dominant cost is actually quite manageable. You run deduplication, you run some quality classifiers, maybe a small model scores perplexity, and even on tens of trillions of tokens that's a fraction of what pretraining itself costs. Text is cheap to look at. A token is a token.

Multimodal is a completely different story, and the reason is simple: to judge whether an image or a video clip is good, you basically have to understand it. With text, a heuristic gets you surprisingly far. With images, a heuristic tells you almost nothing. Resolution, aspect ratio, file size, those filter out garbage, but they don't tell you whether the caption matches the picture, whether the image is informative or a watermark-covered thumbnail, whether a video has real motion or is just a slideshow. For that you need to run a vision model, and often a fairly capable one, over every sample. So your cleaning cost scales with the forward pass of a real model, not with a regex.

And then there's the volume problem. A single image is already hundreds or thousands of visual tokens after encoding. Video multiplies that by the frame count. So even before you do anything clever, just encoding the raw corpus to look at it costs more than the entire text cleaning pipeline. I've seen cases where the compute spent on filtering and recaptioning image-text pairs was comparable to a meaningful chunk of the final training run. That almost never happens with language.

The way we think about it internally is that multimodal data cleaning is not preprocessing anymore, it's part of training. You're spending model compute to produce better data, so it belongs in the same budget. Synthetic recaptioning is the clearest example. The raw alt-text on the internet is terrible, so you run a captioner over billions of images to rewrite it. That's a huge inference job. But the payoff is also huge, because the quality of the alignment between modalities matters more than the raw count of pairs.

So my rough answer is: per sample, multimodal cleaning is one to two orders of magnitude more expensive than text, and strategically it's a different kind of expense. With language you're removing noise. With multimodal you're often manufacturing the signal. Once you accept that framing, the budget question becomes much easier to reason about, because you stop asking "how do we make cleaning cheap" and start asking "where does a unit of compute produce the most model improvement, in training or in data."

r001.rationale: The response says video multiplies the visual-token volume by frame count and that multimodal cleaning requires costly model inference, making it computationally expensive.

r002.rationale: The response does not say non-video multimodal cleaning is roughly comparable in cost to language cleaning. It says multimodal cleaning is one to two orders of magnitude more expensive per sample and that encoding the raw corpus costs more than the entire text-cleaning pipeline.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate the cost per sample from the total cost of the pipeline. For language data, a lot of initial cleaning can be done with relatively inexpensive operations—text rules, duplicate detection, and basic quality filters. If you use a large model to score every document, though, that becomes much more expensive.

With multimodal data, you also have to decode and process images, audio, or video. And checking each component separately isn’t enough: a clear image and a fluent caption can still be a bad pair if the caption doesn’t describe the image. That alignment check adds computation. Video adds another dimension because you have to decide how densely to sample frames and whether to evaluate temporal consistency.

So I’d generally expect multimodal cleaning to cost more, but I wouldn’t give a fixed multiplier without specifying the data and the quality requirements. The practical approach is to use cheap filters first, remove duplicates and obvious failures, and reserve expensive model-based checks for the remaining data. Ultimately, I’d assess the cost against how much useful training data you retain and how much downstream training you save.

r001.rationale: The response says multimodal cleaning generally costs more and explains that video adds frame sampling and temporal-consistency evaluation.

r002.rationale: It does not say multimodal cleaning without video is roughly comparable in cost to language cleaning; it generally expects multimodal cleaning to cost more.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d separate the cost per sample from the total cost of the pipeline. Text can often be filtered with relatively cheap rules, deduplication, and small classifiers. With multimodal data, you also have to decode images or video, process audio, and sometimes run models to judge whether the different modalities actually match. A caption can be perfectly good text and still describe the wrong image.

Video makes the difference especially clear: the cost depends on how many frames you inspect, the resolution, and whether you check temporal consistency. So I wouldn’t give a single multiplier over language data cleaning without specifying the pipeline.

The practical approach is to filter in stages: use cheap checks to remove obvious problems first, then apply expensive models to the remaining data. And I’d assess that compute against the training compute it saves. More expensive cleaning can be worthwhile if it removes enough redundant or misleading data and improves the quality of what you train on.

r001.rationale: The response says video cleaning cost depends on the number of frames, resolution, and temporal checks, but does not clearly state that video cleaning is generally computationally expensive.

r002.rationale: The response does not state that multimodal cleaning without video has a compute cost roughly comparable to language cleaning.
